US Department of Defense: Working Group to Study Implications of Transgender Service

This is certainly interesting, though I think there's a problem. As far as I know, treated transgender people depend on continuous hormone therapy. Wouldn't that be a problem for serving in the army? Excuse me if I'm wrong.

Not at all, I'm glad to help clear things up. You're right in that hormone treatment is a continuous thing, which is a consideration for any soldier. There are many conditions however that require continuous medicine to treat which aren't an issue at all within the military. Anyone with an endocrine disorder of any kind requires hormone therapy, and this has never been a problem at all.

Moreover, in many cases people suffering from dysphoria are given antidepressants to deal with the fact that they can't transition. The Army does not view major depression a career-ender, and is more than willing to hand out powerful antidepressants at a cost to the taxpayer of >$1000 a month, per soldier, for unspecified periods of time. At the same time, the cost of HRT is <$30 per person per month.

Finally, there are many ways to take hormones. Because of Tricare (the military health insurance system), I am unable to take anything but pills for my treatment, as injectables and patches are not authorized. If the military approves transgender service, the healthcare will go along, and I will be able to switch my meds from daily pills to weekly self-administered injections or a patch you only have to change every few weeks.

How to Learn to Code (Thoughts in Comments?)

This video has been shared in a lot of other subverses.

tl;dw: Practice > Theory

I don't entirely endorse it. While I do agree that working toward a goal (fixing a problem you're interested in) is vital, I also think that you can't really do that without at least the basic theory--especially since you're bound to be over-ambitious relative to your skills.

Coding requires a framework of understanding and knowledge, and if you don't have those, you're going to have a really hard time accomplishing anything because you don't know what you don't know. It's like making a song without knowing anything about music theory or music tools (instruments, equipment, programs, etc.). You're going to waste a lot of time fumbling about.

I'd suggest theory is just as important as practice, and the two should go in tandem. While you're trying to create something, you should also be learning about the language/coding in general. When/if you get bored or stuck with the one, switch to the other for a while.

I would say that learning how to google and objectively take in information from the results is a step on getting through learning how to program.

The reason I say this is because you might go right ahead and look for tutorials, examples, etc in the pursuit of your objective, but you may end up being exposed to bad practices that may be hard to remove once you got a hang of what you're doing.
